explain.say: The axolotl, a salamander from Mexico, can regrow a lost leg completely. It starts within hours, when skin cells crawl over the stump and seal it without forming a scar.

faq.a: A blastema is a bud of cells that forms at a wound in animals that can regenerate. Its cells lose some of their adult features, multiply quickly, and then build the missing body part.
asks: What cells rebuild an axolotl's leg?

faq.q: Why do nerves matter for regrowing a limb?
faq.a: Experiments show that if the nerves to a stump are cut, an axolotl's limb will not regrow. Nerves release signals that keep the blastema cells dividing.
asks: Can an axolotl regrow a limb without nerves?

faq.q: How does the new limb get the right shape?
faq.a: Cells in the stump carry a kind of positional memory, knowing whether they came from the shoulder, elbow or wrist. So if a leg is cut at the elbow, only the forearm and hand regrow.
asks: How does an axolotl know what to regrow?
Does the new leg look the same?

faq.a: Axolotls can rebuild parts of their spinal cord, heart, eyes, jaws and even brain, as well as tails and legs, often with no scar.

Our wounds close quickly with scar tissue, which blocks a blastema from forming. Scientists study axolotls to learn which genes and signals might one day help human healing. Young children can sometimes regrow a fingertip.

facts: Axolotls are salamanders native only to the lake and canal system of Xochimilco near Mexico City, and are critically endangered in the wild.
Axolotl limb regeneration depends on nerves; a stump with its nerves cut does not regrow.

quiz.say: What forms at the stump of an axolotl's leg before a new one grows?
quiz.show: Before a new limb grows, the stump forms…
quiz.why: The blastema is a bud of flexible, fast-dividing cells that builds the new limb.

wrong.1: Axolotls avoid scarring, which would block regrowth.
wrong.2: No shell forms; skin covers the stump.
